scope: General educational context only; no personal timing adjudication or source-layer release.

facts.title: Getting started with enrollment timing
facts.question: How does first Medicare enrollment timing work?
facts.text: For most people first becoming eligible at 65, the Initial Enrollment Period is a 7-month window: the 3 months before the birthday month, that month, and the 3 months after. The date coverage begins also depends on when enrollment happens and which enrollment period applies. Current health insurance matters: Medicare.gov checks the kind of insurance, whether job-based coverage comes from current employment, and employer size before giving timing guidance. Do not turn this general explanation into a personal start date, deadline, eligibility decision or permission to delay Part B. A first-of-month birthday has special start-date rules.
facts.summary: The sign-up window and coverage start are different; current insurance helps identify the relevant timing questions.

facts.title: COBRA and Medicare timing
facts.question: How is COBRA different from current job coverage for Medicare timing?
facts.text: COBRA continues a former employer group health plan for a limited time after employment or dependent coverage ends. For Medicare enrollment, COBRA is not coverage based on current employment. For people turning 65 who have not signed up for Medicare, Medicare.gov warns not to wait until COBRA ends to sign up for Part B; COBRA does not extend the time to enroll. A preferred start after COBRA ends is a preference, not a finding that waiting is safe. Use actual Medicare enrollment status and the applicable official enrollment rules to establish a personal next step; do not calculate a personal deadline or effective date from the COBRA end alone.
facts.summary: COBRA and current-employment insurance have different Medicare timing rules. Its end date does not establish when Medicare should begin.
